Limitations.Limitation: The study models a single high shaking demand, so conclusions about social equity may not hold at lower return periods where losses would be settled differently. The team accepted this because behaviour at lower PGA is far more sensitive to spatial variation and much harder to characterise.
The outputs are a relative comparison between policy options rather than an absolute estimate of total land damage cost. Individual cost figures should not be quoted as a standalone number.

Multi-unit buildings, cross-lease and shared land are excluded, so the interaction of multiple sub-caps and settlement split between insured interests is not modelled. This was accepted on the basis that such properties are a small proportion of the population, despite being close to the crux of the policy question.

No retaining wall dataset exists for the study area, so the proportion of properties with walls will rest on an SME estimate varied by suburb. The Wellington City Council database covers council walls rather than the privately owned walls that matter here.

Detecting retaining walls from the LIDAR point cloud will be incomplete because dense vegetation obscures them in exactly the suburbs of interest. The detection rate is itself unknown, so a count cannot be reliably scaled up.

NHC claims cost data may not arrive in a usable timeframe and is not disaggregated by damage type such as retaining walls. The team agreed to plan on the realistic assumption that nothing is received.
T+T's own event data gives better resolution on land damage but carries no cost information, so it cannot inform losses directly.
The GNS slope failure model held in PRUE was discredited by one NHC reviewer and defended by another, so it will be used only as a cross-comparison against the T+T estimate rather than as an input.
The Canterbury earthquake sequence data may not contain enough landslide representation to constrain landslide costs, given it is dominated by flat land liquefaction damage.
Which individual properties are insured is not knowable, so a blanket insurance penetration of 90% is applied as an editable model variable.

The LINZ property ID is the simplest and most stable unique identifier but is less useful to the NHC loss modelling team, who work at claim level. Superseded in part: as of the vul output contract of 2026-09-23, vul carries claim_id and hands it to loss on every table, so the key is no longer minted at the loss boundary. Where vul itself gets claim_id from is still to be settled.
The DEM is a merge of LIDAR surveys flown in different years across the study area, including Wellington in 2023 and Hutt City in 2025.

Driveways are not identified in the LINZ data and are hard to separate from kerbs and footpaths by remote sensing, which matters because driveways are where most retaining walls are. The effect is reduced by properties being small enough that the 8 metre insured land line often reaches the boundary anyway.
Private stormwater and wastewater services are not held on council GIS systems, only the connections, so private service infrastructure cannot be mapped directly.
Land inundated by failure of council retaining walls supporting roads is driven by cost of repair rather than land value, which does not fit the value-based cost logic used elsewhere in the tool.
Geology and geomorphology are taken from the National Liquefaction Model, which simplifies sloping land. It was accepted as a sensible base model rather than an accurate one.
The model will be built quickly on a large number of assumptions, with inputs improved during the remaining time. Outputs should be read as converging on an answer rather than as final.

The public Natural Hazards Portal cannot be used as a claims data source. Its terms of use prohibit automated extraction and incorporation into other databases, and it carries no claim cost, only a binary land damage flag. Claims data must come from NHC directly.

The four territorial authorities were revalued on dates spanning a year, from Wellington City at 1 September 2024 to Porirua at 1 September 2025, across a falling market. Their published averages are brought onto a common date by an index factor that has not yet been signed off by a valuer, and unindexed they would overstate Wellington against the Hutt by roughly 10 to 20 per cent.

Land value is modelled from published QV district averages plus market and engineering judgement until council District Valuation Roll data arrives (T-20). Territorial authority totals are correct by construction because a normalising constant forces them onto the published average; the distribution within a territorial authority rests on judgement and is unvalidated.

The LINZ NZ Addresses layer carries neither a residential or commercial flag nor a land area, so the modelled population is every current land address until parcel data allows the population to be filtered and areas attached.

Phase 1 of the land value model splits land into flat and hill only. The elevated flat premium, sea view, sun exposure and accessibility to centres are declared in the model but not assigned until the DEM phases are complete, so within-suburb variation is absent from the first cut.
The Canterbury land claim costs are in 2010 and 2011 dollars for the 2010 and 2011 events and exclude the 2016 event, so they need escalating before use.
The Canterbury land claim costs exclude GST. If results are presented on that basis it has to be stated to NHC.
The Canterbury land claim costs exclude increased liquefaction vulnerability and increased flooding vulnerability payments, so they cover observed land damage only.
The Canterbury land claim cost rates are being used as placeholders and have not been revalidated for this study. Revalidation was agreed as time-permitting rather than planned.

The Canterbury land damage rates correlate two independent datasets: the per-property field survey of observed damage, and a separate T+T street-level mapping of liquefaction ejecta. The correlation is an assumption the team made, not a property of either dataset.

Inundation repair cost is represented by two rates per square metre — one for volumes removable by shovel and truck, one for volumes needing an excavator — varied by access. Finer variation in volume or method is not represented.

Enabling works and reinstatement are site-specific and priced from the assessor's judgement on the ground — what has to be cleared to get machinery in, traffic management, and occasionally helicopter access. The model can only approximate them from the easy, moderate and difficult bands.

The costing tool's rates are quantity-surveyor derived and refreshed every four months, so any set extracted for this study is a point-in-time snapshot that will drift from the rates NHC assesses against.
Partially damaged retaining walls that would be repaired rather than replaced are not modelled, so every damaged wall is costed as a replacement. John Leeves put partial repairs at about 1% of cases.
Walls already tilted before the modelled event cannot be distinguished from walls tilted by it, so some replacements will be attributed to the event that were already owed.

Inundation removal is folded into the earthworks difficulty rating rather than costed as its own line. The spoil volume sets the rating and buys nothing else, and because the site multiplier reaches wall construction alone, a claim with inundated ground and no retaining wall attracts nothing for the clearing -- real work priced at zero. Whether inundation removal should instead be its own line item, at a rate per cubic metre, is undecided.

Repair cost and undepreciated value come off the same retaining wall square-metre rate, the difference between them being the site multiplier alone. That is how the costing spreadsheet itself works, confirmed 2026-09-23, and it keeps repair cost above UDV by construction. The limitation is specification rather than rates: it assumes the replacement wall matches the one that failed, where in practice a failed wall is often rebuilt to a more substantial current standard, which would warrant a higher rate on the repair side than on the UDV side. The bias has a known direction: settlement is min(repair, cap) less the excess, so understating repair cost can only lower a settlement, meaning the study under-reports NHC's liability rather than over-reporting it.

The insured land extent is clipped to the claim's own property boundary, so a right of way or shared accessway over another title carries no insured land even though the claimant has an interest in it. A fee simple rear lot is unaffected, its leg being part of its own title.
Limitations.Affects: Insured land extent, and every hazard measured against it

Limitations.Limitation: The study does not account for horizontal tectonic movement, such as lateral offset across a fault rupture. For scale, the last Wellington Fault rupture is noted as having had approximately 7 m of horizontal movement.
The study does not account for tsunami or seiche effects. For scale, the 1855 Wairarapa earthquake generated a tsunami approximately 10 m high, with several further tsunamis in later aftershocks.

Site class is assigned from Foster et al. (2019) Vs30 alone, without the profile criteria of TS1170.5 Table 3.3, so rock under weathered cover with Vs30 above 750 m/s would be taken as Site Class I, and Class VII sites take the Class VI spectrum without a site-specific analysis. Over the four territorial authorities Vs30 peaks at 618 m/s, so no cell is Class I at present.
Limitations.Affects: Shaking hazard: site class, and the Sa(1.0 s), PGV and PGA read from it (hazard/shaking s2_site_class, s3_pgv)

Limitations.Limitation: The evacuated and inundated areas assigned to each liquefaction land damage state are judgement ranges set in a project call from the MBIE descriptions of each state, not fitted to observations; the overlap between the two is likewise an assumed 30%.
The Canterbury inundated-land costs carry the effect of the Student Volunteer Army clearing ejecta at no charge, so they understate what clearing inundated land would cost without that labour.

New subdivisions missing from the LINZ property boundaries, addresses and roads either drop out of the claim population or get driveways routed to a distant road. Whether that skews costs in those areas is to be checked once the model runs.

The building use field is too incomplete to filter on, so buildings default to being counted as residential, and sheds, outbuildings and non-residential sites such as the zoo carry insured land and driveways. Treated as a moderate, low-priority source of false positives.

Until claimant-only costs arrive (T-65), every damaged flat land property is charged the Canterbury rate diluted with non-claimants' $0s, rather than a share of them being charged the full rate. The expected repair cost per state is right, but the excess takes more out of many small costs than a few large ones, so settlements come out somewhat low.

The liquefied damaged area takes 30% of the evacuated land as lying under the inundated land (no more than the inundated area itself), so damaged = evacuated + inundated - 0.3 x evacuated, capped at the insured area. This is an assumption about how the 30% overlap agreed on 2026-09-30 is measured, held as EVACUATED_OVERLAP_SHARE in the s2_liq_land_damage config, and is to be verified.

The liquefied land repair rates -- $10.39 per m2 inundated, $19.66 per m2 evacuated and $995 per claim, 2010/2011 dollars excluding GST -- are fitted to Canterbury means estimated from the 50th and 85th percentiles through a lognormal, over Wellington section sizes, and to costs diluted with non-claimants' $0s. They reproduce each state's mean only to within 0.83 (Minor) to 1.24 (Moderate), and price a None claim at the fixed cost alone. To be refitted against claimant-only means (T-65).

Improvements.Improvement: Run a sub-study on multi-unit buildings and the impact of the policy settings on buildings of various sizes.
Improvements.Rationale: Excluded from the main study as too complicated, but no two multi-unit developments settle the same way and the sub-caps are central to the policy question.

Improvements.Improvement: Order a sample of Wellington property files, at roughly $35 plus GST and one working day each, and extract retaining wall and consented works information.
Improvements.Rationale: Parked because there is not sufficient time to access the data within this engagement, though it would need ordering immediately if taken up.

Improvements.Improvement: Analyse the LIDAR point cloud directly to flag vertical surfaces, using return intensity to separate retaining walls from rock faces and vegetated faces.
Improvements.Rationale: The 1 metre gridded elevation model is too coarse to spot walls, but the point cloud may carry the signal; analysing it is complex work in its own right.

Improvements.Improvement: Train an optical model on aerial imagery to identify retaining walls and cut-and-fill slopes, validated against a human-assessed sample.
Improvements.Rationale: A trained eye can pick retaining walls out of aerial imagery, and an existing Auckland Council tool already does this for cut-fill slopes from property file data.

Improvements.Improvement: Incorporate the council retaining wall location model so that failures of road-supporting walls inundating properties below can be represented.
Improvements.Rationale: The last round of landslides included many council wall failures that inundated private property, which the current property-scale logic would miss.

Improvements.Improvement: Obtain claims data from a landslide-heavy event such as the Nelson rain event to supplement the Canterbury dataset.
Improvements.Rationale: Raised by NHC as a way to address the thin landslide representation in the Canterbury data; dependent on the budget being resolved.

Improvements.Improvement: Use the Marlborough District Council online property files as a surrogate dataset for retaining wall prevalence.
Improvements.Rationale: The files are freely available online, although the terrain is not really steep enough to be a close analogue for Wellington.

Improvements.Improvement: Implement the GNS rules for landslide extent, which distinguish smaller and larger failures on the same slope, in place of a per-property assumption.
Improvements.Rationale: Estimating true spatial extent would capture landslides that run across multiple properties, but the rules are complicated and a sensitivity study is quicker to reach a result.

Improvements.Improvement: Extend the analysis to lower shaking demands and lower return periods.
Improvements.Rationale: The main concern raised by the NHC loss modelling team about the single-scenario approach, and the basis for converting damage predictions into land damage vulnerability functions.

Improvements.Improvement: Map driveways by remote sensing so that insured land area and retaining wall exposure can be resolved per property.
Improvements.Rationale: Driveways are where most retaining walls sit, but separating them from kerbs, footpaths and other impermeable surfaces is unresolved.

Improvements.Improvement: Extend the study area to the wider Wellington region, including the south coast of Wellington, the Wairarapa and the Kapiti Coast.
Improvements.Rationale: Cut from the initial extent to stay near population centres and keep the problem tractable, with the south coast explicitly flagged to revisit later.

Improvements.Improvement: Replace straight-line distance to centres with road-network travel time in the land value accessibility term.
Improvements.Rationale: Days Bay and Eastbourne sit about 9 km from the Wellington CBD in a straight line but about a 25 minute drive around the harbour, so straight-line distance materially overstates their accessibility and therefore their land value.

Improvements.Improvement: Use the costing tool's detailed retaining wall build-up, pricing piles, lagging, anchors and drainage individually, in place of the simple square-metre rates.
Improvements.Rationale: The simple calculator was chosen because wall dimensions are guessed rather than measured. If remote sensing later resolves wall geometry, the detailed build-up would be able to use it.

Improvements.Improvement: Give a retaining wall a retained height with some variation in it, rather than one set value per size class. Either draw within the class band or set the height off the slope the wall sits on. Both add spread the portfolio currently gets only from wall length and site ratings, and both would make the priced height round-trip back to its own size class, which the set value for small does not.
Read the PDF-only claim reports. About 380 Kaikoura-list reports survive only as PDFs and are recorded but not read, since the extraction reads Word files only.
Improvements.Rationale: Earthquake claims are the thinnest part of the sample (496 accepted), and these PDFs could roughly double them. Needs a PDF library, which was declined on 2026-09-30.

Improvements.Improvement: Check for T+T project numbers and folders holding land claim reports that the claims lists have not identified, beyond the IAG 1502000, Suncorp 1501000 and EQC 2013 and 2016 programmes already fetched.
Improvements.Rationale: The claims lists come from Site Search exports of known programmes; reports filed under other project numbers would be missed without anyone knowing.

Questions.Question: Can a single property carry more than one land damage claim? A single claim cannot mix settling on market value with settling on repair cost, but whether a property can hold several claims that each make their own election is unknown.

How do the sub-caps interact where a property carries more than one of them, and how does the total cap sit over them? The sub-caps themselves are known: $25k for bridges and culverts, and $50k per dwelling for retaining walls, both plus GST.

Are the enabling works allowances for easy, moderate and difficult sites — nothing, about 15 and about 30 — dollar amounts in thousands or percentage multipliers on the base cost? Chris Ewens gave them as figures and then agreed they were multipliers, while John Leeves was discussing dollar amounts in the same exchange.
Questions.Answer: Multipliers. The bands are the EEE, MMM and DDD rows of the costing tool's combination table -- 0%, 15% and 30% -- so the figures quoted at the demo were percentages on the base cost, not dollar amounts in thousands.

Questions.Question: What are the excess earthworks and constructability percentages for easy, moderate and difficult? Chris Ewens described 15% for each, giving 30% or 45% on the subtotal, then revised it to nearer 0%, 5% and 10%, and separately said individual line items cap at 30%.
Questions.Answer: 0% easy, 5% moderate, 10% difficult, applied to each of three rated factors and summed: construction access, earthworks required, and constructability and reinstatement. The tool enumerates all 27 combinations and every row is that sum, so an all-difficult site reaches 30%, which is the line item cap. Carried in landloss.loss.pricing.

Questions.Question: Does a replaced retaining wall always have to carry a council stormwater connection and a fall-from-height barrier to meet current legislation, and what do they add to the cost?

Is land_slide_total_insured_land_area already the union of the evacuated and inundated footprints, or must loss take that union itself? Where the two overlap the ground is damaged once, so summing the columns would double count it.

Where does the dwelling count come from? Both land structure sub-caps and the excess multiply by dwellings in the residential building, and no table in the vul contract carries one. insured-land.geoparquet carries building_count, which is not the same thing.
Questions.Answer: From the module-level exposure step s3_dwellings_per_property, which counts the address points standing inside each claim property and writes one row per claim. landloss.loss.claims.dwelling_counts reads it onto the claims being settled, refusing a claim with no count rather than defaulting it to one. Note the count is address points rather than self-contained dwellings, so it is a floor on a block of flats and an over-count on a mixed-use building.

Questions.Question: What retained height does each rw_size stand for? The costing tool charges per square metre of wall face, which is retained height by length; rw_length arrives but rw_size is a band (small below 1 m, medium 1 to 2.5 m, large above 2.5 m) rather than a height.
Questions.Answer: Set values for now: small 0.75 m, medium 1.75 m, large 2.75 m. Each is the middle of what its class can contain, the population drawing heights over 0.4 to 3.0 m, and each classifies back to its own size class -- which rules out 1 m for small, since the band is below 1 m and classify_wall_size reads 1 m as medium. Carried as BETA_SIZE_CLASS_HEIGHT_M in landloss.loss.pricing. A size class therefore carries no variation of its own; adding it back is I-14.

Questions.Question: Why are culverts and bridges described asymmetrically in the vul contract? Culverts carry a generic is_damaged and no is_evacuated, while bridges carry is_damaged_by_shaking and do carry is_evacuated.
Questions.Answer: Partly answered: bridges do carry a bridge_id, confirmed 2026-09-23, so every table identifies its own asset. The damage flag asymmetry is still open.

Questions.Question: Can the retaining wall table carry the three site ratings -- construction access, earthworks required, and constructability and reinstatement, each easy, moderate or difficult? loss needs one of each per wall to price a replacement and the vul contract carries none, so no wall can be priced until they arrive. They are a per-wall figure because the multiplier applies to the wall construction subtotal alone. For a real claim they come from a table in the duty geotechnical report; for a synthetic population they have to be inferred, and the inputs -- slope, and the building-to-road path from landloss.exposure.land.driveways -- are already held in exposure.

At what spoil volumes does clearing inundated ground move between hand tools, a mini excavator, and a full excavator with truck cartage? The repository records the distinction only qualitatively -- two rates, 'one for volumes a shovel and a truck can clear, one for volumes needing an excavator' (L-28) -- with no volume attached to either. landloss.loss.pricing currently uses 20 m3 and 200 m3, which are engineering judgement fitted to nothing and set the earthworks rating on every land claim.
Questions.Answer: Not answered. 20 m3 and 200 m3 adopted as a working assumption on 2026-09-23 so the chain could run, reasoned from plant capability rather than from any source, and explicitly not confirmed by NHC.

Questions.Question: Does the T+T database of engineering characteristics of weathered and unweathered greywacke still exist, and where is it held? A T+T capability statement claims 'an extensive database of the engineering characteristics of the weathered and unweathered greywacke rock', built up through geotechnical investigation, instrumentation and laboratory testing; if it survives it could inform the greywacke strength and weathering assumptions in the landslide work.

Do you know who to contact to track down the Precedent/Seismic team's database of slope height and slope angle for greywacke terrain in the Wellington Region? The Transmission Gully proposal methodology (I:\83972\Contractual\Methodology.doc) says the team 'already have' it, and it is also mentioned in projects 24715 and 84947. If it can be found it could inform the slope-angle rules for the landslide model.
Questions.Source: User request 2026-09-30; Transmission Gully proposal (T+T archive job 83972, Contractual/Methodology.doc)

Questions.Question: Which land excess does NHC apply: $500 per dwelling capped at $5,000, as the NHC explainer states and works its examples, or 10% of the amount otherwise payable per claim, floored at $500 and capped at $5,000, as Virginie Lacrosse described on 2026-09-25? The loss module defaults to the explainer's rule and can run either.

Where a property has more than one dwelling or more than one access way, is only the main access way insured land, or can each dwelling's driveway be? Perrie Gilbert read the Act as covering only the main access way; the model is to assume one driveway per property until this is answered.

What share of flat land properties in each liquefaction land damage state (1 None to 6 Very severe) do not go on to make a land claim? The model runs on placeholder drop-out rates of 95%, 75%, 40%, 15%, 0% and 0%, set in DROP_OUT_RATES in the s2_liq_land_damage config, with Severe and Very severe always claimed. They are a tuning parameter to be adjusted on feedback.

Are the Canterbury land damage costs per state (Dec 2016 ILVR rates table) averaged over properties that claimed only, or do they include properties in that state that never claimed as $0? If they include them, the drop-out is already inside the rates and applying the Q-16 drop-out rates as well would count it twice; the T-57 repair rate calibration has to take the same basis.
Questions.Answer: They include them. The rates average over all damaged properties, not just those that lodged a claim -- 'watered down' with $0s, as Virginie Lacrosse described them. She is to supply rates over claimants only (T-65). Until then the drop-out is switched off, since these rates already carry it.

Questions.Question: How much more does clearing liquefaction ejecta cost without the Student Volunteer Army's unpaid labour? The model raises the inundated repair rate by NO_SVA_INUNDATED_MULTIPLIER when NO_SVA is set in the s2_liq_land_damage config, with a placeholder of 1.5.
Questions.Source: Perrie Gilbert 2026-10-02; follows T-57 and L-40

Questions.Question: Should the Waiwhetū Stream count as a lateral spreading free face? It is not named a river, so the NLM's rule leaves it out, but it crosses the liquefiable lower Hutt Valley floor to the harbour at Seaview. Perrie Gilbert has included it by ID (river sections 6818507 and 7212609) provisionally, as the NLM did for the watercourses around Bottle Lake (T-48).
Questions.Source: Perrie Gilbert, QGIS review of the lower Hutt free faces 2026-10-02
